attribution.note: Marcus directly asserts that fabricated legal citations recur routinely.

semantics.note: The normalization captures the recurring legal-citation problem described in context without claiming a particular share of filings.

contract.note: Repeated findings across cases, including lawyer filings, are a fair ordinary reading of routine occurrence. May 2025 is grounded in the surrounding discussion.

evidence.note: Reports at least 23 court-detected hallucination incidents during May 2025, supporting repeated occurrence. The count includes fabricated quotations and other legal authorities as well as case citations.
The May 27 article assigns the 13-of-23 professional-involvement count to the previous month, meaning April. Its metadata and explanation incorrectly assign that count to May.
Documents a May 6 decision sanctioning two law firms for a brief incorporating AI-generated bogus research, establishing a concrete lawyer-involved incident.
Describes rates before spring and in October 2025. These adjacent periods provide context but do not establish the May count.

reviews.rationale: The reported 23 May incidents, together with the dated law-firm sanctions, support recurrent court findings under the contract's ordinary reading. The April professional-involvement count cannot establish May's lawyer share. Neither an overall filing prevalence nor a precise citation-only count is established.
